body: any chance you saved a core dump from the crash?

I found a reproduction:

```
printf "\t" | nvim -u NONE +'set ts=3000000000' -
```

consistently crashes with:

```
nvim: /home/grimy/.nvim/src/src/nvim/misc1.c:1299: plines_win_nofold: Assertion `col <= 2147483647 && (int)col < 2147483647 - (width -1)' failed.
```

On the other hand,

```
printf "\t" | nvim -u NONE +'set ts=2000000000' -
```

just hangs for ever with 100% CPU usage, which is even worse imo.

This still doesn’t explain the original problem, though; I was definitely not playing with ts or very long lines when the crash occured. In the meantime, I think limiting ts to something like 32 would be reasonnable.
@tarruda : core dumps were disabled on my machine at the time the original crash occured.
ok your snippet enabled me to reproduce locally, investigating now
From my tests, it seems that this is [not in vim].

this seems to have been introduced in @2ceb1c74

The crash is caused by `win_linetabsize(wp, s, (colnr_T)MAXCOL)` returning more than INT_MAX which fails the assertion

The following patch fixes both the crash and the hangup; as a downside, lines longer than 32000 columns will be rendered incorrectly.

```
diff --git a/src/nvim/misc1.c b/src/nvim/misc1.c
index 0737cae..660fbb0 100644
--- a/src/nvim/misc1.c
+++ b/src/nvim/misc1.c
@@ -1290,7 +1290,7 @@ int plines_win_nofold(win_T *wp, linenr_T lnum)
    * Add column offset for 'number', 'relativenumber' and 'foldcolumn'.
    */
   width = wp->w_width - win_col_off(wp);
-  if (width <= 0)
+  if (width <= 0 || col > 32000)
     return 32000;
   if (col <= (unsigned int)width)
     return 1;
```

Thanks, I don't think there's any need to have lines longer than 32k(this
should only happen with binary files anyway). Can you send a PR?

The average length of a “line” in a binary file is 256 bytes; 32k lines should be exceedingly rare. OTOH, 32k lines commonly happen in non-pretty-printed XML or JSON.

I can send a PR, but I’m not sure what documentation updates to make. While I can see what the code I changed does, I don’t have enough familiarity with the codebase to understand all the impacts. I made a few tests using a single-line 90k XML file and my patch doesn’t seem to make a difference.

Issue 164 doesn’t actually have much to do with long lines; it’s a bug in the regex engine picker (the regex triggers worst-case performance in the NFA engine, so `set re=0` should pick the old engine).

Issue 274 cannot be reproduced with the default configuration. The reporter probably did something unthinkable like activating syntax highlighting. Syntax highlighting being terribly slow on long lines has been a known issue of Vim for 17 years.

We’re getting off topic: improving Nvim’s behavior with long lines is another issue. This crash/hangup only happens on _ludicrously_ long lines (> 100,000,000 virtual columns).

@chrisbra Thanks.

@Grimy Can we limit to INT_MAX instead of 32000? Also we might want to disallow `'ts'` greater than, say, 1000.

@chrisbra Yes, they are. That’s why Neovim shouldn’t crash or hangup in those cases. My patch fixes that. It doesn’t fix anything else though; Neovim will still have terrible performance in those cases.

@justinmk Limiting to INT_MAX fixes nothing. I picked 32000 because it was already there; the more correct solution would be to limit to $LINES \* $COLUMNS or something like that. With my patch, lines longer than 32000 characters will we wrapped incorrectly on UIs that can render more than 32000 characters (e.g. the TUI with a very small font). This sounds like a minor problem, but I can work on it if wanted.

> Limiting to INT_MAX fixes nothing. 

Ok. That means the bug is in Vim as well then?

Somewhat. `printf "\t" | vim -u NONE +'set ts=2147483647' -` hangs forever with 100% CPU usage, like nvim does. `printf "\t" | vim -u NONE +'set ts=2147483648' -`, instead of crashing like nvim, messes the terminal pretty badly.
To be fair, nvim crashes because it's actually checking for sanity here ;)

Yup, that’s a step in the right direction. It would be better if sanity-checking in nvim didn’t cause data loss. Instead of using `<assert.h>`, Neovim could have its own set of macros that make a save/swap/backup before aborting. (I think I saw an issue about that already, but I can’t find it)
